title: The impact of exposure to air pollution on cognitive performance
research_question: What is the impact of both cumulative and transitory exposures to air pollution on cognitive performance for the same individuals over time in China, particularly across different age groups?

participants.description: Nationally representative sample of Chinese individuals aged 10 and above, from the China Family Panel Studies (CFPS) waves 2010 and 2014.
participants.recruitment: Participants were part of the China Family Panel Studies (CFPS), a nationally representative longitudinal survey.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Air pollution index (API), calculated daily from sulfur dioxide (SO2), nitrogen dioxide (NO2), and particulate matter smaller than 10 µm (PM10). Exposure was measured over various windows: 1-day, 7-day, 30-day, 90-day, 1-year, 2-year, and 3-year means prior to the interview date.

measures.instrument: Standardized mathematics questions (24) and word-recognition questions (34) from the CFPS cognitive ability module. Scores were defined as the rank of the hardest question answered correctly.

findings.quote: long-term exposure to air pollution impedes cognitive performance in verbal and math tests.

findings.antecedent: Air pollution (API) exposure over longer windows (e.g., 3-year mean)
findings.quote: the damage of air pollution on cognitive performance is more sizable when using longer window of exposure measure.

findings.mechanism: Air pollution has a stronger effect on white matter (required more by verbal tests) than on gray matter (required more by math tests).
findings.quote: air pollution exposure appears to exert a more negative effect on verbal test performance than math test performance.
an increase in the 7-d-mean API by 1 SD lowers verbal test scores by 0.278 point (0.026 SD)

findings.antecedent: 1 SD increase in average API over 3 years before the interview
findings.quote: a 1 SD increase in average API over 3 y before the interview is associated with 1.132 points (0.108 SD) drop in verbal test scores.

findings.mechanism: Gender differences in white matter activation during intelligence tests.
findings.quote: Men are more vulnerable to air pollution than women. The gender difference is statistically significant, as shown by the asterisks in Fig. 1A.
Compared with younger age cohorts, the negative effect on the verbal test performance is more pronounced for the older cohorts...
...especially among males. As a result, the gender gap in the decline of verbal skills widens as people age.
Such pattern, however, is less noticeable for the math tests.

findings.consequent: Verbal test scores for men over 44 years old with primary school education or below
findings.quote: the effect for men over 44 y old with primary school education or below is highly negative.

findings.consequent: Verbal test scores for men aged 65 and above with middle school education or above
findings.quote: Among the more educated subsample (Fig. 3B), the negative effect only shows up for men aged 65 and above.

findings.consequent: Verbal test scores for older women, regardless of education
findings.quote: Such pattern, however, is not evident for older women regardless of their education.

findings.consequent: Math test scores by educational attainment
findings.quote: There is no clear difference [for math test scores by educational attainment].

findings.antecedent: API readings on the days after cognitive tests
findings.mechanism: Falsification test to rule out unobserved factors correlated with API readings and outcomes.
findings.quote: all of the coefficients are not statistically different from zero, largely dismissing the concern about potential omitted variables.

findings.consequent: Patience and cooperation during the interview
findings.mechanism: Robustness check to rule out behavioral changes as a mechanism for cognitive performance effects.
findings.quote: None of the coefficients for API is significant, largely dismissing this channel.

findings.antecedent: Reducing PM10 concentration in China to US EPA standard (50 µg/m³)
findings.quote: Reducing the population-weighted annual mean concentration of PM10 over 2014 in China to levels below the National Ambient Air Quality Standards... will on average lift verbal test scores by 2.41 points (or the movement of people from the median to the 63rd percentile...

findings.antecedent: Reducing PM10 concentration in China to US EPA standard (50 µg/m³)
findings.quote: ...and math test scores by 0.39 point (or the movement of people from the median to the 58th percentile in the math test distribution).

findings.consequent: Verbal test scores for less educated men older than 64
findings.mechanism: Projection based on estimated coefficients, highlighting differential impact.
findings.quote: A 1 SD decrease in 3-y-mean API leads to an increase in verbal test scores by 9.18 points (or the movement of people from the median to the 87th percentile in the verbal test distribution) for this group relative to the cohort younger than 25.

findings.consequent: Verbal test scores for more educated older men
findings.mechanism: Projection based on estimated coefficients, highlighting differential impact.
findings.quote: A 1 SD decrease in 3-y-mean API is associated with an increase in verbal test scores by 1.88 points (or the movement of people from the median to the 69th percentile in the verbal test distribution) for them relative to their younger counterpart.

mechanisms: Changes in the brain chemistry or composition (e.g., white matter, gray matter) are likely more plausible channels between air pollution and cognition.
Air pollution has a stronger effect on white matter (required more by verbal tests) than on gray matter (required more by math tests).
Gender differences in white matter activation during intelligence tests may explain differential vulnerability to air pollution.
implementation_implications: The damage on the aging brain by air pollution likely imposes substantial health and economic costs, as cognitive functioning is critical for the elderly for daily errands and high-stake decisions.

The indirect effect of air pollution on social welfare could be much larger than previously thought, suggesting that a narrow focus on health effects alone may underestimate the total cost of air pollution.

tables.description: Estimates of the effect of air pollution on cognitive test scores (verbal and math) using seven windows of air pollution exposure.
key_stats: Coefficients for mean APIs over longer periods are negative and statistically significant.

tables.description: Estimated coefficients on air pollution for male and female subsamples for verbal test scores.
key_stats: Male-female difference is statistically significant for verbal tests.

tables.description: Estimated coefficients on air pollution for male and female subsamples for math test scores.
key_stats: Effect on math tests is more muted than on verbal tests.

tables.description: Estimated coefficients on the interaction terms between 3-y-mean API and age cohort dummies for male and female subsamples for verbal and math test scores.
key_stats: Negative effect on verbal test performance is more pronounced for older cohorts, especially males.

tables.description: Estimated coefficients on the interaction terms between 3-y-mean API and age cohort dummies by educational attainment for verbal test scores.
key_stats: Highly negative effect for less educated men over 44.
Negative effect for more educated men aged 65 and above.

tables.description: Estimated coefficients on the interaction terms between 3-y-mean API and age cohort dummies by educational attainment for math test scores.
key_stats: No clear difference for math test scores by educational attainment.

tables.description: Impact of exposure to air pollution on patience and cooperation during the interview.
key_stats: None of the coefficients for API is significant.

limitations: The exact mechanism linking air pollution to cognitive performance (e.g., specific brain chemistry changes) was not tested and is left for future research.

Potential for unobserved time-variant factors (e.g., migration to different cities for better jobs and air quality) that could correlate with both cognitive test scores and air pollution exposure, despite controlling for individual fixed effects (addressed by falsification tests, but acknowledged as a concern).

paper_metadata.crossref_abstract:
Significance
          
            Most of the population in developing countries live in places with unsafe air. Utilizing variations in transitory and cumulative air pollution exposures for the same individuals over time in China, we provide evidence that polluted air may impede cognitive ability as people become older, especially for less educated men. Cutting annual mean concentration of particulate matter smaller than 10 μm (PM10) in China to the Environmental Protection Agency’s standard (50 μg/m
            3
            ) would move people from the median to the 63rd percentile (verbal test scores) and the 58th percentile (math test scores), respectively. The damage on the aging brain by air pollution likely imposes substantial health and economic costs, considering that cognitive functioning is critical for the elderly for both running daily errands and making high-stake decisions.
